ACTIVE SCENE — Adventurer · ENGAGED
The road took him down between hedged fields, and the walls of Glassmere grew as he walked—grey stone, old, patched in places with newer brick, the top of a bell tower showing beyond them. Carts and foot traffic thickened as the verge gave way to packed dirt; a drover passed with geese in wicker cages, complaining to nobody about the price of feed. The gate had no queue worth the name at this hour. Two guards in the city's colors leaned by the arch, watching traffic with the boredom of men halfway through a shift. One glanced at Alaric's staff and robes, marked him for a student or a hedge mage, and looked back at the road. "Mind the carts," was all he said, and waved him through. Inside, morning had the city working. Bakers' smoke hung over the first streets; a water-carter splashed through the gutter muck; shutters clattered open above a chandler's shop. Stone gave way to timber-framed fronts as the street bent downhill, and the noise of a market square rose somewhere to the left. Nobody paid a blond stranger with a staff much mind. He found the Guild by its sign rather than any grand front—a crossed sword and arrow cut into a hanging board above a wide door, wedged between a cobbler's and a moneylender's window. The door swung open at a push into a long hall that smelled of tallow, old leather and somebody's wet boots. A big hearth held last night's embers. Benches ran down the middle, half filled with adventurers nursing breakfast or checking over gear, and a scarred wooden counter stretched along the far wall where a stout woman with grey-streaked hair was taking a complaint from a mud-splattered carter. Behind her, a board of notices stood in plain view. The carter was still talking—something about a bridge, and what he'd been promised—when the woman's eyes lifted and found Alaric over his shoulder. She gave him the measuring look the counter gives everyone new.

extra.display_text:
The clerk took the slip down from the board, stamped it, and passed it over the counter with his plate. "Glimmerdeep, level one. Signed and yours." She pulled the board copy off and pinned his name in its place. "You've got until the moon turns, then it goes back up." She leaned an elbow on the counter. "You know where it is? Cleft in the hills, a morning's walk north, where the stream comes out of the rock. The academy keeps the cleft—" She angled her head toward the leather-cuirass man. "Doran, tell him about the cleft." Doran swallowed his eggs and came over, wiping his fingers on his trousers. "Academy warden at the cleft mouth, Warden Hallis. Shows his seal to him, signs the cleft ledger, and he'll point you down the right gallery. Beetles and slimes, mostly, on level one. Beetles chew the crystal, slimes eat the beetles' leavings—nothing clever down there, but a slime's no joke in a tight tunnel if you let it get round you." He scratched his jaw. "Whatever crystal you knock loose is yours to pick up, that's the academy's custom. Deep galleries are theirs; don't go past the warden's marks." He looked Alaric over—the staff, the robes, the fresh plate. "Solo, are you? Level one's honest work for a Novice, long as you don't get greedy past the marks. Anyroad, that's the shape of it." The clerk slid a stub of chalk across the counter. "Mark your name on the slate when you leave the city, so the desk knows who's out on what. Glimmerdeep's an easy road—north gate, follow the stream. Any other questions, ask now or ask the warden at the cleft."

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The clerk took the slip down from the board, stamped it, and passed it over the counter with his plate. "Glimmerdeep, level one. Signed and yours." She pulled the board copy off and pinned his name in its place. "You've got until the moon turns, then it goes back up."

She leaned an elbow on the counter. "You know where it is? Cleft in the hills, a morning's walk north, where the stream comes out of the rock. The academy keeps the cleft—" She angled her head toward the leather-cuirass man. "Doran, tell him about the cleft."

Doran swallowed his eggs and came over, wiping his fingers on his trousers. "Academy warden at the cleft mouth, Warden Hallis. Shows his seal to him, signs the cleft ledger, and he'll point you down the right gallery. Beetles and slimes, mostly, on level one. Beetles chew the crystal, slimes eat the beetles' leavings—nothing clever down there, but a slime's no joke in a tight tunnel if you let it get round you." He scratched his jaw. "Whatever crystal you knock loose is yours to pick up, that's the academy's custom. Deep galleries are theirs; don't go past the warden's marks."

He looked Alaric over—the staff, the robes, the fresh plate. "Solo, are you? Level one's honest work for a Novice, long as you don't get greedy past the marks. Anyroad, that's the shape of it."

The clerk slid a stub of chalk across the counter. "Mark your name on the slate when you leave the city, so the desk knows who's out on what. Glimmerdeep's an easy road—north gate, follow the stream. Any other questions, ask now or ask the warden at the cleft."

The slate by the door carried a scatter of names in different hands; Alaric chalked his beneath them and pushed out into the morning. The north gate was busy with carts—grain, wool, a load of split firewood—and the gatewarden waved him through without a second look. Past the walls the road ran thin and packed beside the stream, willows leaning over the water, the hills ahead rising green-grey against a sky scudded with high cloud. A shepherd's dog trotted the verge, looked at him, thought better of it and dropped behind a hedge. By the time the sun stood near noon the road had worn to a path, the stream narrowed, and the hills closed in close enough that the water's noise came back off rock. Then the cleft. It split the hillside like an axe-cut, a dark seam perhaps two cart-widths wide, and the whole stream ran out of it over pale stones, loud in the narrow ground. The rock around the mouth glittered faintly where the light caught it—crystal veined through the stone itself. A rough stone hut stood against the cleft wall, smoke from its chimney, a bench outside, a ledger chained to a post beside the door. A woman came out of the hut wiping her hands on a leather apron. Grey at the temples, forearms like a smith's, an academy seal worked in blue on the apron's chest. She looked at Alaric, then at the staff, then at the Guild plate he'd have to show anyway, and waited for him to produce it before she'd touch the ledger. "Guild, is it. Name, and which level."

The wave left his staff as a widening ring of pale light, and it crossed the chamber before the first beetle so much as paused its rasping. It took all four at once. The nearest burst like a dropped jar, shell cracking into shards that skittered across the crystal floor. The second folded mid-click, legs folding under it. The third and fourth were flung off the fallen vein, rolling, smoking faintly where the magic had gone through the smoked glass, and then they too stopped moving. Four clicks' worth of silence, then only the drip of the stream somewhere behind. Warmth ran up his arms and settled—a level, then another, then a third, the System's chime sounding soft and clear in the crystal dark. The shards on the floor lay still. Loose plates of chitin and a pair of intact venom sacs had already found their way into his pouch the way the System's loot did, without his touching them. The chamber held nothing else living. The crystal sheet at the far wall glowed on, indifferent, and a passage opened beyond the fallen vein, deeper blue paint faintly visible on its wall.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The wave left his staff as a widening ring of pale light, and it crossed the chamber before the first beetle so much as paused its rasping.

It took all four at once. The nearest burst like a dropped jar, shell cracking into shards that skittered across the crystal floor. The second folded mid-click, legs folding under it. The third and fourth were flung off the fallen vein, rolling, smoking faintly where the magic had gone through the smoked glass, and then they too stopped moving. Four clicks' worth of silence, then only the drip of the stream somewhere behind.

Warmth ran up his arms and settled—a level, then another, then a third, the System's chime sounding soft and clear in the crystal dark. The shards on the floor lay still. Loose plates of chitin and a pair of intact venom sacs had already found their way into his pouch the way the System's loot did, without his touching them.

The chamber held nothing else living. The crystal sheet at the far wall glowed on, indifferent, and a passage opened beyond the fallen vein, deeper blue paint faintly visible on its wall.

extra.display_text:
The beetle husks gave up nothing further; the System's picking-over had been thorough, and what remained was shell dust and splinters going soft already, the crystal of the chamber slowly eating them back. The chamber itself was another matter to walk, if not to carry. Crystal chips lay everywhere the fallen vein had shed them, some no bigger than a fingernail, some the length of his hand, all dead to the light—the glowing stuff stayed in the living walls and would not come away. He pried at one seam near the far sheet and the chip came free dull, worth a cartload of nothing. At the chamber's edge, though, half-tucked behind the fallen vein, something man-made caught his eye: a rusted pick-head, long abandoned, its haft gone to rot, and beside it a canvas satchel stiff with damp, the strap crumbled when he touched it. Inside lay a clay jar of pitch-sealed wax—still good—and a folded square of oilcloth wrapped around nothing but a broken trowel. Whoever had worked the vein had left in a hurry, or worse, and taken nothing but what they carried. No bones. No marks on the walls but the warden's blue paint and old chisel scars. Beyond the fallen vein the passage went on, the glow of the crystal thickening down its length, the air carrying the first faint sourness the warden-woman had warned of—slimes, somewhere ahead.

The climbing passage took him up in a long, easy rise, wide enough for two abreast and dry underfoot, the floor sprinkled with grit that his boots found quietly. The blue warden's mark followed at intervals, a fresh brush-stroke on the crystal at each bend, and once, where the wall had spalled away, an older mark beneath it—a chiseled arrow, the miner's work, pointing the same direction up. Halfway along, a side hollow opened to his left, shallow as a cupboards depth: old candle stubs fused to a ledge, a coil of rope gone stiff, nothing else. The air up here tasted cleaner, the slime-sourness left behind below, replaced by a dry mineral smell like a struck flint. The passage ended at a lip of stone, and beyond it the floor opened out into a broad gallery where the ceiling rose again and the crystal grew tall along the walls in curtains, casting the whole space in a dim underwater glow. The sound reached him before the sight of them: a slow, gritty grinding, like a millstone turning over sand. Two of them worked the gallery floor below his lip of stone. Mineral slimes, each the size of a hound, gray-green and translucent, lumps of crystal ore suspended inside them like fruit in jelly. They moved without hurry along the base of the wall, and where they passed, the stone beneath them came away faintly pitted, fresh-scraped trails shining behind them in the glow. One of them paused, quivered all through, and began easing itself toward the foot of the slope. The other ground on along the wall, its back to him still.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The climbing passage took him up in a long, easy rise, wide enough for two abreast and dry underfoot, the floor sprinkled with grit that his boots found quietly. The blue warden's mark followed at intervals, a fresh brush-stroke on the crystal at each bend, and once, where the wall had spalled away, an older mark beneath it—a chiseled arrow, the miner's work, pointing the same direction up.

Halfway along, a side hollow opened to his left, shallow as a cupboards depth: old candle stubs fused to a ledge, a coil of rope gone stiff, nothing else. The air up here tasted cleaner, the slime-sourness left behind below, replaced by a dry mineral smell like a struck flint.

The passage ended at a lip of stone, and beyond it the floor opened out into a broad gallery where the ceiling rose again and the crystal grew tall along the walls in curtains, casting the whole space in a dim underwater glow. The sound reached him before the sight of them: a slow, gritty grinding, like a millstone turning over sand.

Two of them worked the gallery floor below his lip of stone. Mineral slimes, each the size of a hound, gray-green and translucent, lumps of crystal ore suspended inside them like fruit in jelly. They moved without hurry along the base of the wall, and where they passed, the stone beneath them came away faintly pitted, fresh-scraped trails shining behind them in the glow.

One of them paused, quivered all through, and began easing itself toward the foot of the slope. The other ground on along the wall, its back to him still.

RECOVERY — HP 90→105/105, MP 68→135/224
He settled against the wall beside the lip of stone, staff across his knees, and let the quiet take the gallery. The crystal curtains glowed on, steady as moonlight through water. Water dripped somewhere behind the far wall, unhurried, counting out the time. The dead slimes below went on dulling. Their sheets of fluid thinned and stiffened at the edges, the color fading from gray-green toward chalk, and the scattered ore lumps sat where they had rolled, catching the glow. Nothing else came up the slope. Nothing came down it either. Once, faint and far off, something scraped at stone on a deeper level—a sound with no urgency in it, gone again before he could guess at its shape. The rest did its work quietly. The knot of spent mana behind his eyes loosened first, then unwound altogether, the deep tiredness of casting lifting from him the way fog lifts off a river. By the second hour his breathing had slowed and the ache had gone out of his shoulders entirely, and the cold of the stone through his clothes mattered less. He felt whole again, rested to the bone, his mana pooling back to its full quiet depth. Two hours. The gallery had not changed except in small ways: the slime trails fully set now, dry and matte, and the light no different than before. Daylight above, if it still shone, was hidden behind however much rock lay between here and the sky.

He rose, took up his staff, and went on past the dried slime trails and down the slope beyond, deeper into the glow. The gallery narrowed and turned, the crystal curtains giving way to ribbed pillars that met the ceiling in smooth flutes. His footsteps came back at him soft and doubled, and the drip from before faded behind him until the only sound was the faint glassy creak of crystal warming or cooling in the rock. Old tracks crossed the floor once—shallow grooves, beetle-run, worn smooth by many small feet—and passed in a clause, leading somewhere he did not need to follow. The air grew cooler and faintly sweeter, like the smell of a winter stream over stone. The passage opened without warning into a wide, low chamber, and he understood at once that he had arrived somewhere that mattered. The far wall was not wall anymore. It was crystal grown thick and tall as a barn's inner face, veined with pale blue light that pulsed—slowly, steadily, like something breathing in its sleep. Veins of that light ran out from it across the floor and up the side walls, thinning as they went, the way roots thin from a tree. The whole room was lit by it, and the temperature here was different too, warmer, almost body-warm where the light ran densest. And on the crystal face itself, things moved. Beetles clung to the glowing wall in dozens—bigger than the ones he had killed on the way in, their chitin catching the pulse of the light so the whole cluster rippled between silver and shadow. They worked at the face with their mandibles, scraping, harvesting, and none of them had yet turned his way. Beneath the largest cluster, half-embedded where the crystal met the floor, sat a shape too round and too large to be any of the workers: a swollen, gleaming bulk the size of a plump hound, its shell veined with the same blue light, faintly luminous itself, its small head buried in the crystal it fed from. The Glimmer Queen, mother of everything that crawled this level, feeding in the open.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
He kept low and moved along the edge of the chamber, footfall by footfall, until the Queen's pale bulk sat far across the room—long range, well beyond the reach of anything it might throw at him. The beetles went on scraping their wall, blind to him.

He leveled the staff and the lance went out.

The flame crossed the chamber in a single breath and struck the Queen's swollen body dead center, and the crystal around her lit white with reflected fire. The crack of it rolled through the room. Her shell split along the impact point, chitin weeping molten light, and the whole great bulk convulsed—a shudder that ran from her buried head down through the half-embedded rear of her, her legs scraping furrows in the floor as she tore herself half free of the crystal face.

She had not known he was there. Now she knew.

She came at him fast—faster than anything that size had a right to move—her heavy legs hammering the stone, blue light flaring along her cracked shell with every furious stride. She closed the distance in seconds, her mandibles working, until she stood only a few paces from him, near enough now that he could see the wound smoking, near enough to smell the scorched resin of her shell.

Behind her the beetles boiled off the wall, streaming down in a glittering fall.

Her head came low, legs braced, weight coiling.

QUEST READY FOR TURN-IN — Clear Glimmerdeep Grotto Level 1 · The Glimmer Queen is dead and her swarm scattered; the chamber is his and level 1 of the Grotto has nothing left that rules it.
The bolt took her high in the head where the first one had cracked her, and this time there was nothing left to hold her up. It burst through, and the light in her veins went out all at once, blue fading to dull gray down every vein of her shell. Her legs folded sideways, first the front pair, then the rest, and the great body came down on the stone with a wet, glassy crash that shuddered through the floor. Her mandibles clicked twice against the crystal, slow, weaker, then stopped. The hiss behind her broke apart. The swarm poured down almost to her body and then the charge simply died—mandibles lowering, legs turning, the whole glittering stream folding back on itself. They scattered toward the walls and the dark seams of the chamber, climbing over one another in their hurry, and within a dozen breaths the floor held only the dead Queen and the fading pulse of the crystal she had fed from. Whatever held them together had died with her. The warmth of her blood on his hip was still there, the bite still raw, but the room had gone quiet. The veined light in the far wall breathed on, slow and steady, keeping its own time. In his pack, unnoticed until now, something new sat alongside the rest: a heavy plate of the Queen's chitin, iridescent even in the dim light, and a smooth pale stone that hummed faintly against the pouch's other contents. And somewhere behind his eyes the System settled its accounts—strength pouring in, three times over, his body remade a little harder, a little sharper, while the wound on his side went on bleeding as it pleased. The chamber was his. Level 1 of the Grotto had nothing left in it that ruled it.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The bolt took her high in the head where the first one had cracked her, and this time there was nothing left to hold her up.

It burst through, and the light in her veins went out all at once, blue fading to dull gray down every vein of her shell. Her legs folded sideways, first the front pair, then the rest, and the great body came down on the stone with a wet, glassy crash that shuddered through the floor. Her mandibles clicked twice against the crystal, slow, weaker, then stopped.

The hiss behind her broke apart. The swarm poured down almost to her body and then the charge simply died—mandibles lowering, legs turning, the whole glittering stream folding back on itself. They scattered toward the walls and the dark seams of the chamber, climbing over one another in their hurry, and within a dozen breaths the floor held only the dead Queen and the fading pulse of the crystal she had fed from. Whatever held them together had died with her.

The warmth of her blood on his hip was still there, the bite still raw, but the room had gone quiet. The veined light in the far wall breathed on, slow and steady, keeping its own time.

In his pack, unnoticed until now, something new sat alongside the rest: a heavy plate of the Queen's chitin, iridescent even in the dim light, and a smooth pale stone that hummed faintly against the pouch's other contents. And somewhere behind his eyes the System settled its accounts—strength pouring in, three times over, his body remade a little harder, a little sharper, while the wound on his side went on bleeding as it pleased.

The chamber was his. Level 1 of the Grotto had nothing left in it that ruled it.

extra.display_text:
He went through the chamber slowly, staff in hand, giving the fallen Queen a wide berth at first. Her body was already cooling; up close the cracked shell dulled further by the minute, the iridescence draining out of it like breath off a window. What she had left in her was in his pack. Prodding at her only confirmed it—no cache beneath her, no passage hidden under the bulk of her, just stone and the thick smell of scorched resin. The crystal face at the far wall drew him longest. The veined light ran steady beneath its surface, blue-white, and where the Queen had half-buried herself the crystal was scarred and pitted, grooves worn smooth by generations of her feeding. Nothing loose came away. He tried a piece at the edge and it held fast, humming faintly against his palm before he let it be. Whatever this seam was, it would take more than hands to quarry it. The rest of the chamber was floor, wall, and the swarm's leavings: shed plates of chitin scattered near the walls, brittle and dull, most of them crumbling when he picked at them. One or two of the better pieces were sound enough, though nothing beyond what his pack already carried. A dark seam in the northeast wall, where the beetles had fled, let out a thin draft of cooler air—it was the way on, if there was a way on, down into the deeper levels of the Grotto. The passage back the way he had come lay open behind him, the tunnel quiet now. Nothing else. No bones, no old gear, no marks of anyone having come this way before him. The chamber had been the Queen's, wholly, and everything of value in it had died with her. The bite at his hip pulsed when he straightened. The blood had begun to dry stiff in his clothes.

The way out was quieter than the way in. He climbed the passage past the warden's chalk marks, crossed the pillar-field chamber with its shattered slime residue already drying to crust, and came up through the crystal gallery into gray afternoon light. The keeper's stone hut stood open at the cleft mouth, woodsmoke rising, but she was inside with her back to the door and he was on the road before anything passed between them. The walk to Glassmere ran through falling light and thinning traffic—carts headed the other way toward evening markets, a shepherd driving his flock off the verge. Once, at a bend by a stream ford, a pair of drovers argued over a mule that refused the water, and one of them looked up as if to hail him, then thought better of it and went back to shouting. The mule was still refusing when Alaric passed out of earshot. The Guild hall's lamps were just being lit when he came in. Warmth and noise rolled out to meet him: the hearth going, a knot of adventurers by the board, and Doran still at his usual table near the fire, a bowl in front of him and a story half-finished for whoever would listen. The stout clerk with the grey-streaked hair looked up from her ledger as he reached the desk. "Back already." She took the contract slip, turned it over, and her eyebrows rose at the seal. "READY, is it. The Grotto's first level." She glanced at him—at the dried blood stiff down his side, at the staff—then dipped for her strongbox and counted out a little stack of copper. "Sixty. The Guild thanks you for the work." The coins slid across the counter, and she pulled the ledger toward her to make her entry. "Now." She looked up again, pen hovering. "You'll be wanting the board, or a bath, or a bed, or all three. Which is it?"

extra.display_text:
The clerk's pen stopped mid-word. She looked at him over the ledger for a long moment, then snorted—a short, unbothered sound—and finished her entry before she answered. "Charm costs extra here." But the corner of her mouth had shifted, a little. "Inn you want is the Drowned Lantern. Two streets down toward the river, sign's a lantern half-sunk in a blue wave, you can't miss it. Marda runs it. Beds are clean, the bath water's actually hot, and she doesn't water the ale. Tell her Brenna sent you and she'll charge you the same as everyone else, but she'll be friendlier about it." She tapped the ledger closed with her pen. "Brenna. Since you asked." She gave him the measuring look again, the one from this morning, though it sat differently on him now that the ledger said sixty copper paid out and a Grotto cleared. "You look like you've been rolled down a hill, so mind how you go. If you're back on the board tomorrow, I'd eat first. Dead men bargain poorly." Behind him, Doran's voice had trailed off mid-story. The man was watching Alaric over his bowl, eyes moving from the dried blood down his side to the staff and back, doing his own arithmetic about the Grotto and how the stranger had come back from it before dark.

name: Avereth Engine Test v4
mes:
The clerk's pen stopped mid-word. She looked at him over the ledger for a long moment, then snorted—a short, unbothered sound—and finished her entry before she answered.

"Charm costs extra here." But the corner of her mouth had shifted, a little. "Inn you want is the Drowned Lantern. Two streets down toward the river, sign's a lantern half-sunk in a blue wave, you can't miss it. Marda runs it. Beds are clean, the bath water's actually hot, and she doesn't water the ale. Tell her Brenna sent you and she'll charge you the same as everyone else, but she'll be friendlier about it."

She tapped the ledger closed with her pen.

"Brenna. Since you asked." She gave him the measuring look again, the one from this morning, though it sat differently on him now that the ledger said sixty copper paid out and a Grotto cleared. "You look like you've been rolled down a hill, so mind how you go. If you're back on the board tomorrow, I'd eat first. Dead men bargain poorly."

Behind him, Doran's voice had trailed off mid-story. The man was watching Alaric over his bowl, eyes moving from the dried blood down his side to the staff and back, doing his own arithmetic about the Grotto and how the stranger had come back from it before dark.

extra.display_text:
He pulled the sheet from its nail and carried it back to the counter. Brenna read the title, then read him—the whole of him, staff and robes and all—slower than she'd read the paper. "The moors job." She said it flat. "Three ghouls, out past the eastern shepherds' marks. That's a Veteran's paper, most days, and it's sat up there three days because the Veterans who'd want it are busy elsewhere and everyone else has sense." She dipped the pen anyway. "You're the one who took the grotto job yesterday, aren't you. Red eyes. I thought I'd written that name before." She logged the entry, pressed the Guild's seal into the wax, and held the slip out without quite letting go of it. "Listen. Ghouls don't tire, they don't bleed out sensible, and they're strongest at the cairns themselves, where the ground's all loose stone and holes for the ankle. If you mean to go alone, go by the road east to the shepherd's shelter first and let them know—old Hesk runs sheep out that way and he'll point you to which corner of the field the trouble's been in. Cheap knowledge, free even, he likes the company." She let the slip go. "And if you get out there and it's worse than three, walking away is allowed. The Guild pays for finished work, not for graves." Doran set his bowl down with a clack. "Eastern road's past the south gate. Half a day's walk, the moors after that." He looked Alaric over the same way Brenna had. "Huh. Good luck to you."

The south gate let him out onto the eastern road with the morning still cool and the dew not yet burned off. The way ran through farmland first—hedgerows, a boy driving geese, a wagon heaped with turnips whose driver gave him a nod and nothing more—and the staff on his back drew a glance or two from field hands but no conversation. By midday the farms thinned and the road climbed into rougher country, gorse and grey stone, the wind picking up with nothing to break it. Somewhere past the second mile of it a chimney smoke rose thin against the sky, and the track bent toward it whether he liked it or not, because the shelter sat where the track forked. The words were barely out before the dogs' ears pricked, and so Alaric gave them nothing else—no goodbye, no wave—just turned along the fork that climbed east, weight rolling heel to toe on the flint, and the old man's squint tracked past the spot where he'd stood without catching him. One dog snuffed at the dust where his boots had been, lost the thread, and lay back down. By the time Hesk thought to look at the road, the road held nothing but heat shimmer. The rise took effort, gorse grabbing at his hem, and beyond it the land sank into a shallow bowl of grey. The black pool sat at its near edge, still as poured ink, midges hanging above it in a column. And past it, the cairns—hundreds of them, some knee-high, some man-high, tumbled piles of stone dotting the field like a flock of petrified sheep, all the way to the great central mound with its leaning slab tilting off the top like a crooked door. Noon sun beat flat on the field. Nothing moved between the stones. But the ground near the big cairn had burrow mouths under its lip, dark gaps in the shadow, and a smell drifted off the bowl of the land that didn't belong to sheep—old meat and wet earth. He went down the slope low and slow, choosing his footing among the stones, and the field swallowed the sound of him. Close up, the leaning cairn showed claw-grooves raked pale into its stones, and from one of the burrow mouths came a sound like a slow wet snore. He crouched behind a waist-high pile of rock, thirty paces out, unseen, the noon light flat and bright on the burrow mouths and on the open ground between.

The rise took effort, gorse grabbing at his hem, and beyond it the land sank into a shallow bowl of grey. The black pool sat at its near edge, still as poured ink, midges hanging above it in a column. And past it, the cairns—hundreds of them, some knee-high, some man-high, tumbled piles of stone dotting the field like a flock of petrified sheep, all the way to the great central mound with its leaning slab tilting off the top like a crooked door.

Noon sun beat flat on the field. Nothing moved between the stones. But the ground near the big cairn had burrow mouths under its lip, dark gaps in the shadow, and a smell drifted off the bowl of the land that didn't belong to sheep—old meat and wet earth.

He went down the slope low and slow, choosing his footing among the stones, and the field swallowed the sound of him. Close up, the leaning cairn showed claw-grooves raked pale into its stones, and from one of the burrow mouths came a sound like a slow wet snore.

He crouched behind a waist-high pile of rock, thirty paces out, unseen, the noon light flat and bright on the burrow mouths and on the open ground between.
